delay_records.current_state: Roosendaal maintains the authoritative database of all confirmed delay records at ericr.nl/wondrous/delrecs.html. As of March 2026, records are confirmed up to the range being computed by the distributed project.
delay_records.key_observation: Approximately 7-8 delay records per decade (power of 10) are found, implying that on average a delay record is 1.36 times larger than its predecessor.

known_benchmark_records.note: a(8) of A284668 - the classic benchmark

delay_records.target: Compute a(19) of OEIS A284668: the number below 10^19 with the highest Collatz total stopping time

verification_frontier.barina_technique: GPU-accelerated sieve with 1335x total acceleration over naive CPU. Distributed across European supercomputers. Also found 4 new path records during verification.
verification_frontier.roosendaal_distributed: Active distributed project checking ranges in units of 10^12 numbers per block. As of March 2, 2026, all blocks up to 35,900 (35.9 × 10^15) completed for class records.

sieve_methods.description: Use modular arithmetic to precompute which residue classes mod 2^k converge quickly. For k=32, can skip ~99% of numbers.

shortcut_tables.description: For residue class r mod 2^k, precompute the symbolic result of k Collatz steps: n -> (a*n + b) / 2^k. Allows processing k bits in one arithmetic operation.

combined_step.description: Since 3n+1 is always even when n is odd, combine into (3n+1)/2 in one step. Reduces step count by ~37%.

tail_optimization.description: Once trajectory drops below known-verified threshold, stop. All numbers below 2^71 are verified (Barina 2025).

binary_tricks.description: Process trailing zeros with bit shift. Count trailing zeros with CPU instruction (ctz). Use arbitrary precision only when needed.

oeis_a284668_analysis.target_a19: Numbers below 10^19 (~63 bits). Need to scan ~9 × 10^18 numbers (those between 10^18 and 10^19) and compare against a(18)'s delay of 2283.
oeis_a284668_analysis.feasibility_analysis: Using Barina's reported rate of 1.31 × 10^12 numbers/sec on GPU, scanning 9 × 10^18 numbers would take ~79 days on a single GPU. However, with aggressive sieve (99%+ skip rate), CPU multicore with 20 cores and shortcut tables could potentially do this in hours to days.
oeis_a284668_analysis.key_insight: We don't need to compute full trajectories for most numbers. The sieve eliminates numbers whose trajectory is guaranteed to be short. We only need full computation for the ~0.01% that survive the sieve.
